en: The Attainment of Self-Sovereignty:
Now begins the section on Superimposition (Adhyāropa).
He gazes with a smile at the Daughter of the Mountain, who, fearing the Lord of Serpents as his matted locks are stirred by the current of the Gaṅgā, clings to Him.

May Śiva—the moon-crested one, whose form is supreme bliss—grant us liberation from the darkness of delusion, as he delights the people who bow before him with the playful glances of his side-long looks. || 1 ||
Remembering again and again the fear of birth and death, having developed a sense of world-weariness, meditating repeatedly upon Paśupati, the beloved of Umā who dwells within;
and drinking again and again the stream of the nectar of supreme bliss—I bow down ever more deeply to the pair of lotus feet of my own guru. 2.

I worship that Lord of Teachers, by whose grace I am he who is the Supreme Brahman—the inner Self—whose nature is truth, knowledge, and bliss; from whom the universe arises, in whom it dwells, and into whom it finally dissolves; which is free from the destruction of duality as its limit; and which shines alone, devoid of sorrow, throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. 3.
For those whose inner selves are purified by study, sacrifice, giving, vows, recitation, meditative concentration, and observances; who contemplate this world as being devoid of essence;
who are free from attachment and aversion; and who conduct themselves without fear—for such seekers of liberation, we shall speak of something exceedingly sweet, beneficial, and heart-pleasing. 4.

Having known the Lord, there is the removal of all bonds; "there is no other path"—by such repeated statements, once it is established that knowledge is the direct cause of liberation, the fact that [ignorance] is a superimposition (adhyāsa) is proven by the very force of the sense. || 5 ||
Since knowledge does not dispel that which is real, whereas objects such as a jar—which are destroyed by action—are false and thus destroyed by action rather than by knowledge;

and since this distinction is established, it follows from the words of the crest-jewels of the Vedas that bondage is known to be destroyed by knowledge and is therefore false. Once this is established, the collection of ritual actions is not capable of removing it.
For this bondage of ignorance ceases not without the cessation of karma-born sensations; does a snake born from a garland ever go to its end through prostrations, mantras, medicines, and the like?

Having thus resolved, one should shake off the bond of karma according to the prescribed method—just as a serpent sheds its skin—and, having approached the venerable feet of the Guru as the means to knowledge, one should strive while rendering service. 7.

Some understand that action alone, when freed from desire, is the means for attaining the exalted state; they further assert that both that [action] and its worship are combined as the supreme means for liberation.

Others, however, conjecturing according to their own views that it is both knowledge and action, do not immediately accept those two [positions] here, on account of the scriptural statement "only from knowledge. || 8 ||

The world of the ancestors is to be attained through sacrifices, and the world of the gods through knowledge; or rather, let the exhaustion of the impurities of the mind here be the goal prescribed by the Smṛtis for those two.

From the statement "by sacrifice" and so forth, let there be the desire to know (vividiṣā) as the fruit, or let knowledge itself be the result; for immortality comes from knowledge alone—surely the female rabbit does not give birth to a lion cub. || 9 ||

"I am a seeker, a capable twice-born, wise, intelligent, skilled in ritual action, authorized, peaceful, self-controlled, a wandering mendicant, and one who has reached the highest state; such a knower of Brahman is qualified for the knowledge of Brahman.
Desiring to express such a distinction, he would—alas!—desiring to quench his thirst, drink both cool water and fire together as the combined cause of liberation. || 10 ||

Furthermore, that knowledge—which consists of the realization of the identity of the Self with Brahman, whose nature is non-dual, whose essence is the density of bliss, and which is infinite pure consciousness—arises for one of excellent intellect from such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). However, because of the deep-seated habit of superimposing the body and other such things [upon the Self], even though it has been heard, the state of being Brahman is not easily conceivable for oneself; therefore, one must properly investigate it through the instructions of a teacher who has realized the truth. || 11 ||

Some say the body is the self; others, the sense-organs; still others, the vital breaths, the mind, or the intellect—some regarding it as momentary and others as permanent; some say it is consciousness devoid of happiness; others that the self has the nature of both insentience and consciousness; others that it is consciousness like a diamond yet insentient; and others that it is the non-dual reality of truth, knowledge, and bliss. Among these, what is the certain conclusion?
Some say that the self is atomic; some that it is the size of the body; others that it is all-pervading; and still others have declared it to be an object of the mind, or always inferable.

Others say it is an object of consciousness, while yet others say it is the supreme inner light. Such being the case, repeated inquiry by means of scripture and reasoning is appropriate for one who desires to know.

Thus, some have declared *prakṛti* to be the cause of the universe; some, atoms presided over by the Lord; some, mere momentary cognition; others, the void (*śūnya*); some, Brahmā; some, time (*samaya*); some, chance (*yadṛcchā*); others, karma; and still others, Brahman as variegated by *māyā*. Therefore, even that [last-named] must be investigated.

That which is the origin, protection, and even the destruction of the worlds; that which has the scripture as its sole source; that which is omniscient; that whose nature is the non-dual consciousness of innate bliss through Māyā—that Brahman is self-luminous and the ultimate ground of the intent of the words of the crest-jewels of the Vedas. It is this very Self, knowing which the virtuous here cross over the ocean of birth and death. 15.
The Pradhāna proclaimed by the Sāṅkhyas as the cause for the creation of these worlds is not acceptable here; nor is the Īśvara described by the logicians capable of effecting such a purpose.

Neither is the atom (aṇu) mentioned by the followers of Kaṇāda, the Buddhists, or the Jainas, nor is it a void devoid of a witness. Therefore, the cause is our own, established as the Supreme Brahman declared in the Śruti. || 16 ||

If the non-conscious Pradhāna were to act by its own nature, there would be the consequence of constant creation, since even Niyati (the principle of necessity) is preceded by creation and cannot exist prior to it.

Furthermore, bondage would be without cause; how then could there not be a lack of distinction between bondage and liberation? Moreover, the wise man does not desire a liberation devoid of bliss; therefore, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is flawed.

Furthermore, if the non-agent were the enjoyer, there would be the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done; moreover, what kind of enjoyment could there be for one who is unattached and devoid of any modification? What purpose, then, would the object of enjoyment serve? What kind of non-discrimination belongs to whom, and how could that non-discrimination become the cause of enjoyment? For whom would there be discrimination, and what would happen because of it? Indeed, for one who reflects thus, even for a Brahmin, this is difficult to explain. (18)

The Pradhāna of the logicians, being devoid of body, organs, and qualities, would not be capable of presiding [over evolution]. If it were to possess a body and sense-organs, there would be the consequence of experiencing the fruits arising from its own past deeds.

If it were to create this world so full of suffering, the faults of immoral conduct and cruelty would attach to it. Furthermore, for one who desires the results of karma, there would be the fallacies of infinite regress (cakraka), circularity (avasthiti), contradiction (hati), and futility (viphalatva). ||19||

If there were an omniscient Lord, desiring all things, endowed with all capacities, and eternal, then every effect would exist eternally, and creation, maintenance, and dissolution would occur simultaneously.

Furthermore, in the creation of the universe, there would be a dependence on external material causes for the body, organs, and intellect; thus, inference would be devoid of logic, and even the "activity" [of the Lord] would be discarded, since activity is established for the sake of a purpose. (20)

Why should there be motion in two atoms? And how, being devoid of resistance, could they then coalesce? Or how could a third effect arise from them; why would it not be large, given its spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*)? Why would a large object arise from them? Furthermore, why should this [large object] alone be eternal and not those [atoms]? And why is the atom partless? Tell me, O proponent of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavādin*). (21)

"O dull-witted one, you who speak of the external objects of enjoyment as a momentary collection of atoms, and [assert] that the internal enjoyer is a composite of the five aggregates—let such a Vedabāhya (outsider to the Veda) be questioned by the Sugata: 'Is this measured by some other means of knowledge, or is it merely your own bold assertion, or is it a babble born of delusion, or perhaps a desire to deceive the world? " (22)

How can there be a state of aggregation for atoms that are devoid of motion and are themselves perishable? How could a non-distinct aggregate reach the status of an object, and who is it that constructs the aggregate?

How is there a conjunction of the aggregates, how many are they, what is the nature of the enjoyer, what is the stream, and to whom do enjoyment and liberation belong? Tell me, O dull-witted one, by what means could your doctrine be fruitful?

If you claim that the two-fold origination [of suffering] does not proceed from ignorance and the rest because each individual member, while not perishing, lacks the power to produce [the next], then how can an effect be unrelated to its cause?

If it were causeless, there would be the futility of instruments and a contradiction of your own thesis; furthermore, how could there be a threefold classification in the case of non-existence? Thus, the deluded teacher’s prattle is utterly false. (24)

That which is established by mental cognition cannot be sublated; otherwise, how could there be various cognitions? If objects were denied, how could there be sublation, given that external objects are not seen [to exist]? Furthermore, the word "outside" (bahiḥ) would not attain its well-known meaning.

Cognitions must be known as distinct; otherwise, from where would the various latent impressions (vāsanās) arise? Moreover, the previously mentioned defects apply to a momentary consciousness; therefore, the Vijñānavāda is destroyed.

That which is established by consciousness cannot be sublated; otherwise, how could there be various cognitions? If objects were denied, there would be no contradiction regarding external things, nor would the word "external" attain its well-known meaning.

Furthermore, how could there be distinct cognitions, or from where would diverse latent impressions (vāsanās) arise? Moreover, the previously mentioned defects apply to momentary consciousness; therefore, the Vijñānavāda is destroyed.

The birth of an entity from non-existence is not perceived anywhere; for from that which is devoid of distinctions, a manifold variety could not arise. Furthermore, there would be the cognition "it is non-existent" regarding everything that is permeated by it.

By what means is the manifestation of non-existence [established] for you? Why is everything not produced from everything as you desire? O dull-witted one, why do you strive to destroy yourself without effort?

If a single object were to be sevenfold, then there would be a sevenfold nature; and if that were so, why would objects such as the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva) not likewise be so? Furthermore, the world would become chaotic. There would be doubt due to contradiction, or else, if you claim certainty, there would be a lack of order regarding bondage and liberation. Thus, your doctrine of non-absolutism (anaikāntya-vāda), stripped of its clothing, appears as nothing but the ravings of a madman. (27)

Thus, even that which is proclaimed by Hiranyagarbha and others as the cause of the world is not worthy of respect; for from whom has such a birth been understood through the Śrutis, and whose lifespan is measured and fixed?
Since the Vedic Word (Brahmavāṇī) teaches his possession of knowledge and other qualities, therefore, Brahman alone—variegated by Māyā—is the appropriate and sole scriptural source.

Why is one person miserable while another has been endowed with happiness since birth? From what cause does activity arise today, and from where does even the body come? Furthermore, why does the deceased not know his own nature?

If you say that the disparity seen in lamps, seeds, sprouts, and so forth is produced by karma—given that equality is known to exist when causes are identical—then the existence of the self must have been established even prior to birth.

If you claim that perception alone is the single means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then explain how your own statement is a valid authority; for if it is faulty because its object is merely probable, then why is the Veda not also powerful and faultless?

Indeed, there is no perception without the senses, nor is the validity of perception easily established by you alone; since cognition does not have the power to know anything other than itself, you are therefore a speaker of falsehoods. (30)
"The notion of a self in the body—such as 'I am fair, stout, young, and clever'—is established among people by their very nature; therefore, this view of yours is fruitless.

If [this view] has arisen from hatred toward the Vedas, alas, it is not at all a valid means of knowledge rooted in hatred. By fate you alone have been destroyed; why then, O rogue, do you proceed to destroy others? (31)

O fool, why do you consider this body—which is produced from semen and blood, inert, filled with food, subject to six transformations, composed of skin, bone, sinew, flesh, entrails, marrow, and blood, extremely insignificant, abounding in diseases, and which at the departure of life becomes nothing more than earth, dung-worms, or ashes—to be "I"? By whom have you been deceived? 32.

In the doctrine that the elements (khānām) constitute the self, there would be the undesirable consequence of bodily dissolution due to the fault of multiple masters for each restricted function; furthermore, those who have attained union [with the self] would die as mute regarding their own nature.

Moreover, the expression of what has been seen or heard would not be possible, nor could a collective [self] be defined; there would be no personal observer, and fear would arise because there is no distinction between lying down and dying. 33.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the Self, because it is insentient, because it exists through the acquisition of functions by means of eating and drinking, and because in deep sleep one has the cognition "I am unmoving" [indicating the Self remains while the breath moves].

Furthermore, the Creator [desiring his own departure] sustains this [breath] until death; therefore, there exists another, denoted by the word "living being" (*jīva*), who protects his own abode, the radiant *ekahaṃsa* (the solitary swan). || 34 ||

Because it is the means for the arising [of the world], because it is the cause for the perception of purity and impurity through its nature as food, and because of the scriptural teaching that after those two—bondage and liberation—the embodied soul becomes identical with that; and because the mind, which is measured by the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, is not the Self:
for when the group of organs dissolves in deep sleep, the mind is at peace, yet upon waking from that sleep, there is the recollection of the bliss of sleep. Thus, even the mind is not the Self. (35)

That consciousness which is stable is here identical with the mind; moreover, it would possess a manifold nature because [the mind] consists of many elements, and because the bondage of the self is heard of in scripture as being due to the notion of that [manifold mind].

Although its role as a charioteer is assigned to it within the body-chariot for the sake of its own experience and liberation, there exists within it another inner self, consisting of pure consciousness, who is the witness of this [mind] and whose body is conditioned by it. (36)

If the self were atomic and of the nature of consciousness, you would have no experience of cold throughout the entire body; nor, in the case of non-difference [from the body], could there be a lack of cognition, for there is no other quality that pervades the whole body as its grasper.

If, on the other hand, there is difference, how could the atomic quality of consciousness pervade the entire body? Or by what means is the atomicity of your self established? It is not by the scriptures, for those [scriptures] do not culminate in [the doctrine of] infinity. || 37 ||
How could the conscious self not be one? And how then could it be an object? What are its two parts? What is yoga, and what is the self? Why is there insentience in that which is sentient?

Of what nature is its agency, and how does it maintain this collection of instruments? O beloved of the gods, this reality of the individual soul is difficult to define for those who are like beasts, devoted only to ritual action. 38.

If you claim that the majesty of souls is due to the body, then because the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is common to all, there would be no regulation of experience; for by what [distinction] could the mind also be made distinct for each? If you say that the plurality [of souls] is established through the limiting adjuncts of the bodies, then since the difference [between souls] is already established, such distinctions would be useless here, whether that difference be proven or unproven. || 39 ||
Furthermore, conjunction is not possible in a partless self, for the mind is itself partless;
nor is there any substance that is both partless and eternal, nor is cognition its property, since cognition would otherwise be insentient. (40)
If you were yourself ignorant and blissful during deep sleep, how could you, being inherently insentient, remember "I am awake"?
By what means could you, lacking a witness, know that "this one" or "that one"—these numerous cognitions—I have seen for a long time? 41.

Therefore, there exists another witness whose nature is unimpaired vision, who remains unattached even while moving within the three cities—the continuous stream of the arising and destruction of desire and the rest, as well as the senses, the mind, and the intellect. 42.

When the sun, moon, fire, and the light of speech have been stilled, and the collection of sensory organs has entered into extinction, the inner self—the element of consciousness whose objects consist of latent impressions manifested by its own light, and which is free from all attachment—is proclaimed by the Vedas. 43.

He who perpetually expands that [intellect] by means of the group of external objects and the senses, and by means of the intellect, through his own light—that Self, which has not been apprehended by these [faculties] directed toward the external, is to be known as the lamp within the body and the house. 44.
That inner self, who is dearer than one's own home, wealth, or children, and whom others consider dear because of their love for him;
who is the ultimate limit of all that exists for the sake of another, having disregarded all other interests—he indeed should be known as the ocean of happiness. 45.

This pure Self, through the superimposition of the attributes of limiting adjuncts, identifies itself with "this" (the body and mind), just as one might falsely, out of delusion, attribute the qualities of the various waters—such as increase and decrease—to the moon reflected in them. 46.
Because of the experience "I am ignorant," beginningless nescience—which is rooted in consciousness—shines forth as an object within consciousness, like darkness obscuring the moon.
Alas, this mind, having been projected by consciousness itself, manifests and causes further delusion; it is indeed difficult to define.

That Māyā, which—like consciousness within the manifestation of consciousness—is inherently capable of effecting the distinction between itself and the other even while there is no actual division; and which is most skillful in bringing about the union of the possible and the impossible, produces delusion through its illusory play. 48.
Superimposition (adhyāsa) is indeed clearly experienced as the cognition of something in that which it is not, regarding an object not previously apprehended;
for example, [the thoughts] "I am ignorant," "I am a man whose strength has failed," "I am poor," or "Alas, how shall my sons live?"—all of which refer to the inner self (pratīci). 49.

"I am pure, joyful, and firm; I am wise"—thus he ascribes the attributes of the Self to the body. And "I am stout, fair-complexioned, handsome, and clever"—thus he measures the attributes of his own body as his own.

With its form enveloped by the mutual superimposition of the real and the unreal, it undergoes a multitude of worldly misfortunes born of various existences, like fire entering a mass of iron that is struck by a hammer. (50)

Since superimposition (adhyāsa) is clearly observed even between two objects that are diametrically opposed—like light and darkness—in the form of "I" and "mine," the wise have no doubt regarding this matter.

Because there is no other way to account for the perception of blueness in the sky, and because the cognitive process of animals and humans is identical, it is established that all empirical experience is rooted in superimposition. 51.

Through dharma one attains divinity, but through sins one goes downward again, obtaining bodies such as those of stationary beings and the like; not perishing, one may at some point obtain human birth through both of these—namely, action and knowledge.
By means of knowledge alone, one reaches the state of the Lord and is liberated; yet someone who is attached therein returns to rebirth, and thus the world wanders here in this difficult cycle.

There is suffering from falling into one's own hell; there is great suffering in the womb and in various hells; in childhood, there is only suffering due to lack of independence, hunger, the influence of planets, disease, and bloodletting; in youth, there is the suffering of indignation, greed, vice, humiliation, anxiety, and poverty; in old age, there is suffering through grief, delusion, the decay of the senses, and disease—thus, in this endless cycle, there is extreme suffering. (53)

Thus, for that living being who, bound by karma, wanders helplessly through multitudes of births and—due to the power of ignorance—neither knows the end of suffering nor remembers the succession of his own births, the crest-jewels of the Vedas, the Sūtras, the Bhāṣyas, and other works have been diligently engaged to consecrate him in the kingdom of his own Self by means of the method that pacifies the root of all misfortune. (54)
The chapter on superimposition (adhyāropa) is complete;
now begins the chapter on negation (apavāda):
She holds in her beautiful hands a book that is supreme, fearless, and sublime, as well as a rosary of beads, a jewel, and bracelets.
May the Goddess of Speech, adorned with white garments, as beautiful as jasmine and pearls, and possessing a face like the moon, dwell within our speech. || 1 ||

I worship in my own mind the one with the curved trunk (Vakratuṇḍa), who has made the moon his crest-ornament, whose beautiful trunk is fondled by the hand of Gaurī, and who is fierce in quelling the obstacles of the multitude of devotees. 2.
The lotus, having risen from the mud, does not long possess its splendor; it is crushed by swarms of bees and trampled by their feet, and its stalk is covered in quivering thorns.

Thus, as if laughing at the moon—which, though victorious, is subject to the fate of waning—by the beauty of its rising nails, I perpetually worship the beautiful lotus-feet of the most excellent and glorious Teacher, who remains ever silent in his vow. 3.

The definition of causality that has been stated—consisting of the nature of being the material cause and the agent—like the moon [reflected] in water, points toward its own supreme locus through its state of detachment;

and thus the object of definition is that which has the form of existence, consciousness, and bliss, devoid of all duality, extremely subtle, declared in the mantras as truth, knowledge, and so forth, beyond all mind and speech, and situated in the cave of the heart. || 1 ||

The immutable Brahman produces the universe not without *māyā*; yet that [universe] is false, because it is established by words [only], because it is understood through the consensus of others, and because of the scriptural teaching on its cessation.

That very *avidyā* is the illusory object; though unreal, it is thoroughly understood and capable of producing effects—the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Therefore, like the variegated color of a peacock's feather, the expansion (*vivarta*) of the consciousness of Brahman is profound and mysterious. || 2 ||

Since the entire universe arises from Being (*sat*), is sustained by Being, and is dissolved therein, therefore it is nothing other than pure Being (*sanmātra*), just as the modifications such as the jar and the cup are not different from clay.

If there were a difference [between Being and the world], then Being would be non-existent; yet if that [world] is Being, then no difference exists at all. Difference and non-difference are contradictory; for difference cannot have its foundation in an undivided reality. || 3 ||

Indeed, difference perceived in that which is non-different is false, like the manifold nature of the moon; likewise, non-difference in that which is different arises from the same cause, and thus there is no intrinsic difference between things.

If difference were established by means of attributes (*dharma*), then alas, when those attributes themselves are either different or non-different, the distinction between attribute and substrate (*dharmidharmivyavasthā*) is certainly not recognized in the world. (4)

That which is non-different by its own nature cannot possess difference through another; nor could one thing be distinguished from another merely through the difference of others. How then could properties be diverse if they are non-different from the substrate? If difference resides in distinct loci, then that distinction must depend on a difference in the substrates themselves. If it is established as residing in the self [of the substrate], then there is no distinction; if it resides in each other, the stability of their existence is destroyed. Thus, such difference is difficult to define. (Verse 5)

This difference is to be known by a cognition produced by a cognition whose object is the counterpart of the distinct substratum; thus, the establishment of the difference between the substratum and so forth would require yet another [difference], leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If there were no difference in the substratum and so forth, alas, the cognition of difference would be false; if there were a difference, the aforementioned defects would arise. Since there is no other way out, difference is indeed false. (6)

In a substance, there is no connection with difference, for that which is devoid of designation (nirupākhyam) is not a positive entity (bhāva), nor is it a distinct non-entity (abhāva), because it is equal [to both], nor does it possess the nature of either, as it is a non-meeting of both.

Furthermore, there is nothing whatsoever existing between existence and non-existence that constitutes a relation between them; yet, even in the absence of a relation, difference is perceived through illusion, like silver in mother-of-pearl. Thus, difference is cognized. || 7 ||

Because conjunction and the like are impossible, there can be no differentiation; for it is not within the range of the senses. Pervasion does not belong to that which is unattached, nor is there any similarity, as it is far removed from the purport of words.
There is no absence of proof that serves as proof, nor is there any other proof for this; nevertheless, it is directly perceived—like a city of one's own illusion—and thus it is truly false. 8.

An external object does not arise from mere cognition; for it to become an object of perception for others, it would have to exist as a single entity, and not as both [simultaneously]. Thus, the manifestation of those two as distinct is false. Otherwise, there would be a confusion of duality and so forth. Indeed, your postulation of a "perceiving intellect" (apekṣābuddhi) dependent on the state of prior non-existence is untenable. All of this should be applied gradually to the case of separateness (pṛthaktva) as well. || 9 ||

The effect is not something other than its cause, because it is not apprehended as separate; for there is no distinction between the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*hetu*). If there were such a distinction, the state of inherence (*samavāya*) would not exist, as it would not have attained that condition. Otherwise, in the case of an effect such as gold, there would be the undesirable consequence of an increase in price due to a doubling of its weight. Furthermore, if there were a difference based on a change of state, then men would also become distinct entities through the difference between their states of rest and motion. (10)

When one reflects in the mind upon the state of a lump of clay as being a pot, the cognition of cause and effect arises; yet when one clearly perceives it as merely clay, there is neither cause nor effect.

In the same way, for one who contemplates in the mind the world-illusion (māyā) and the phenomenal universe (prapañca), Brahman is the cause of the universe; but for one who keenly perceives it as pure Being (sanmātra) of a single form, there is neither the illusion nor the universe. || 11 ||

Whatever exists—such as water-jars, excellent mortars, and so forth—and whatever was previously heard, all that appears like clay pervading a pot or a pan; it is the Truth. Just as a snake is imagined upon a rope, the entire world is imagined within That;
by its very nature, it is nothing but That. For if there were any difference from That, this whole universe would be non-existent, whereas in non-difference, it is indeed That alone. || 12 ||

The single reality of Brahman, through its manifestation as shell-silver and the like within the sphere of empirical usage, produces the cognition "this world is real" by means of the initial illusory perception;

yet, for as long as it appears, in the second case [the silver], it is renowned as if it were a red color—like madder—on a cloth or crystal, such that one thinks "the cloth is well-dyed red," though on the crystal it is false. (13)

Even though there is a single uniform essence of reality, consciousness, and bliss, due to the presence of other states—unreality, insentience, great suffering, and delusion—a conceptual distinction in form arises within the scope of the conventional usage of statements such as "Being, Consciousness, and Bliss.

Just as the existence [of nacre] shines forth in the case of "this is nacre," being permeated by its conceptualized counterparts like "non-nacrity," so too, through the subduing of the veil of Māyā, it appears as consciousness and bliss. || 14 ||

When asked, "Who is the king in this assembly? he who is shimmering upon the back of an intoxicated elephant, amidst a network of pearls, at the base of a moon-white, glittering parasol—he immediately recognizes that specific person as "the King. By saying all this with reference to one [person], while looking at another of a different kind, he knows, "This other one is not the King. || 15 ||
Just as descriptions of physical characteristics define a particular individual by distinguishing him from those who merely desire to know,
so too the scriptures concerning the creation of the universe point toward the Supreme, the flawless mass of consciousness.

Although here, as in the case of the words "That" and "Thou," there is no cognition of an impossibility of syntactical connection (*anvayānupapatti*), nor is there a single unified referent among the word-meanings such that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) would apply to the individual words; nevertheless, those words—conveying distinct meanings yet joined in relation to one another—would, by following the introductory context and other criteria, collectively indicate that non-dual Reality which is Being and Consciousness (*saccidadvaya*). || 17 ||
In the waking state, where the delusion of duality is nourished by external means of knowledge such as perception through the senses, the Śruti is suddenly incapable of awakening one to non-duality;
therefore, with the intention that this entire collection of empirical objects is false, it composed a systematic exposition characterized by the cycles of creation and dissolution.
Having described Brahman as existence-consciousness-bliss, beyond all speech and mind, situated within the cave of the five sheaths, and eternally transcendent of the world;
and having set aside both "the real" and "the unreal," the Śruti itself declares that which is inherently real—the non-dual—clearly and explicitly. (19)
"The knower of Brahman reaches the Supreme"—that indeed is the realization characterized by the non-duality of Being and Consciousness, and that realization is within the cave of the heart;

for the sake of attaining one's own true nature, the Śruti, having thus declared this, undertook this creation of the universe in order to establish the reality of non-dual Being, for otherwise such establishment would not be possible. (20)
In the beginning, there was indeed only one, and no other; having beheld this entire universe, he created it by entering into its body.
As he wandered through his own three abodes, he became aware of them and, having attained all desires by means of his own self, he became immortal. (21)
Having conceptualized the entire universe as the two-fold form of Brahman— divided into gross and subtle, and manifest and unmanifest—
the *Kāṇva* and *Vājasaneyaka* Śrutis, after negating every form by declaring "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), have established the non-dual reality in its entirety.
Since this entire world is known through the power of His awakening, the intention here is to explain that [Reality] by means of the words "Being, my dear, is [all this]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

Therefore, preceded by the creation and the contemplation [of the Self], the illustrations of clay and so forth are employed with the desire to express the unity of the world; for in this way, they attain logical consistency. (23)

This entire world is born from Being, exists in Being, and dissolves into Being by its own nature; being devoid of independent existence, it is all merely Being appearing as something separate and false.

For that which is imagined as separate does not exist, like the water in a mirage in the desert; thus, the reality is non-dual Being alone—this is the intended meaning of the statements regarding creation.

Having proclaimed that which is to be attained through the supreme knowledge—subtle, devoid of attributes (dharma), and imperishable by nature—the Fourth Voice declares that from that [source] the entire world arises as a falsehood; for it is clearly established that "That alone is Truth," and by means of pure consciousness, That itself becomes manifest, eternally attained. 25.
Having divided the past, future, present world, and that which is beyond, according to its four quarters, each consisting of the essence of the True Praṇava;

and having dissolved each preceding quarter into the succeeding one, the Atharvaṇa Śruti has proclaimed the non-dual Śiva as the Fourth (turya), which is indefinable and the very nature of one's own self. 26.

In this very manner, one should harmonize the multitude of scriptural passages concerning creation heard here and there with the non-dual Reality through the diligent study of the cosmogonic processes and so forth, by means of both reasonings and scriptures. Indeed, that [Reality], when grasped through its extrinsic definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa), results in the determination of the existence of the object to be defined and the exclusion of the three-fold doubt regarding its nature. || 27 ||

The true characteristic of this [Self] is the nature of non-dual bliss consisting of existence and consciousness; it is not found in that which is unreal, non-manifesting, or devoid of happiness, for such states do not constitute the goal of human endeavor.

Therefore, its identity with that [Self] must be realized. Nor is there any destruction of non-duality by words that have acquired their status through distinctions imagined according to various prohibitions and injunctions; indeed, I have already explained this properly before. (28)
Its reality is established by its subtlety, like the sky; by its state of being the substratum for the blueness of the world, which is neither distinct from nor excluded from it;

by its being the witness of all, as it is the ultimate limit of all sublation; by its lack of attachment and non-contradiction; by its omnipresence and its nature as the Self; by the absence of any other seer; and by hundreds of clear scriptural statements as well as one's own direct experience. (29)

Because it is the Self, because it is the Seer, because of its sovereignty over all, because of the teaching that it is the source of the scriptures, because of the instruction regarding desire and longing, because of the statement that its nature is light illuminating the moon, the sun, and so forth, because of the teaching that it is the immediate witness of both good and evil deeds, and because of words such as "all-knowing" and "all-seeing"—and indeed by hundreds of clear statements—it is established that its very essence is Being and Consciousness. (30)

Because it is the ultimate limit of the excellence of happiness; because of the scriptural declarations that it is an ocean for the drops of all happiness; because of the doctrine that it is attainable by the liberated; because its nature is an infinite, supreme abundance of bliss;

because of the doctrine that it is the inner self (pratyak) of all; because of the doctrine that it is the treasure-chest, the abode, and the bride; and because Brahman is described as "bliss" even in the state of deep sleep—it is therefore eternally of the nature of bliss.

That which is declared here as the definition of Brahman—the state of being of one essence with truth, consciousness, and bliss—is equally present in the individual self (jīva), for that [self] is also the inner witness of all perceptions, and sublation and so forth are impossible for it.

This is because it is the primary locus of love; because no difference in substance is established despite the distinction of limiting adjuncts; because of the teaching that it is a portion of Brahman; and because the body, organs, and the faculty of sight are self-luminous [insofar as they reveal it]. (32)

Since this observer of sublation is not himself seen to be sublated even while being sublated along with those objects of his own experience that are being sublated, how could he, being the very nature of vision, conceive of a sublation of himself?

Because there is no measure for a difference in vision, because vision is never an object of vision, and because he is changeless—therefore, this inner self (pratyagātman) is the eternal reality, without limit.
That which shines as the uniform "I, I" across diverse states such as childhood and so forth, perceived directly like objects in a waking state; that which one knows even while asleep;

and that which, even when the ego-sense is stolen away, remains the witness of the unrobbed bliss of deep sleep and the rest—since the seer's vision is never lost, scripture also declares that this is the inner self (pratyagātman), whose nature is pure consciousness. || 34 ||

That which one calls "other than the Self" and says will obstruct one's pleasure, and that which [the scripture] declares to be unified with the Wise One during deep sleep through the nature of bliss and consciousness;

that which is known as the desire for what is favorable to oneself in the three worlds, and the wish to abandon what is contrary to oneself, and the longing "May I always exist"—that is this inner Self, whose essence is happiness. (35)

When the reality of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) has been thus thoroughly investigated through the words of the scriptures and the teacher, as well as through reasoning and direct experience, and when their essential identity has been skillfully realized;

then the sentences such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), whose inner meaning has been grasped through the examination of their beginning and end and other means, are truly capable of making one realize one's own true nature without any obstacle.

That which existed as the Real prior to creation, and that light and so forth which it created—into that [light] the individual soul (jīva) entered; and when [the soul] had entered, it projected all that which is unreal, namely name and form.

That [Reality], which is to be known by the word "That" (tat), is declared by the word "Thou" (tvam) to be the individual soul named Śvetaketu. Thus, the word "art" (asi), conveying the eternally established meaning of the sentence, expresses the present identity.

The first type of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two names is held here to have as its object the sublation (*bādha*), superimposition (*adhyāsa*), a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), or identity (*aikya*). Among these, it cannot be superimposition, for in that case the scriptural statement would be a futile effort;

furthermore, because meditation and the like are not enjoined, there would be the defect of resulting in a non-eternal fruit. Nor can it be identity, for identity is impossible between two contradictory things. Thus, by force of logic, the position of the identity of the underlying reality (*vastvaikya*) is established.
The meaning of these two words here is inconsistent, for two entities possessing contradictory properties cannot attain unity;
nor is there metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā), because there is no utility in connecting them as roots and so forth, even though their respective meanings are joined together. (39)
Nor is a third [meaning] established here as suitable for the connection, like the bank of the Ganges which is attached to the word;
nor is there any justification for determining that one of the two words possesses the mark of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). || 40 ||
Neither is its other form, which is like another, established by perception, nor does there exist a future state for it;
for the abandonment of what was heard and the assumption of what was not heard are improper. Thus, a partial indication (bhāga-lakṣaṇā) is indeed appropriate for both. 41.

Having abandoned the collection of conflicting attributes, O witness of the limited intellect, perceive that which is the seat of infinite, dense consciousness; then, like the sentence "This is that," one should join the two words together in reference to the indivisible reality.

In order to destroy the notion of being beyond perception and unattained regarding the Supreme, and the notions of incompleteness, suffering, and delusion regarding the Inner Self (Pratīc), and to express His own extraordinary essential nature (ātmatattva) in the state where both [the Supreme and the Inner Self] desire one another; || 43 ||
In this context, "having an indivisible object" (akhaṇḍārthatā) consists either in the words having a non-composite true meaning or in their having no other referent.
For this is well-known in such sentences as "The moon is the most excellent light," which brings about the cognition of the moon alone. || 44 ||
The distinctions such as excellence, luminosity, the state of being the moon, and the exclusion of others were not at all asked about;
nor does there exist a verbal cognition regarding an object not intended to be inquired about; therefore, from that sentence, there arises the awakening of the mere moon. (45)
He who, having first emitted the world, entered into its body; he who is the self of the five elements, of gods, humans, and animals;
by whom one sees, speaks, and perceives—he is that Supreme Self, whose power consists solely of pure consciousness. 46.

That which was the uncreated world, enveloped in darkness from the tips of the nails, and that which entered the body and was yet incomplete—precisely that is my dearest, the supreme in the ultimate sense; "I am Brahman," for he who knows it becomes that very all. 47.

"That which is manifested here within the person in the cave of the heart, and that which is the ground of immeasurable bliss in the orb of the sun—one is that," so some have declared; they clearly state their identity, and through the knowledge of that, the dissolution of the world occurs therein. 48.
Indeed, you were always the Existent (Sat); having conceived that which is not real as being the face of light, you became the individual soul (jīva).
Cast off this sprout of the body and behold your own Self: "Thou art That," the Reality which is Being, Consciousness, Bliss, and non-dual. 49.
Just as flavors merge into wine once it is prepared, so too do people, upon attaining the singular state of bliss in deep sleep, remain unaware;
yet when they emerge from that state, they again become partakers of manifold suffering. That which is the supreme Brahman—you are That, and you are never a sufferer. 50.
Just as the waters, having been drawn away by clouds, are led into the state of rivers and the like and thereby lose their identity as the ocean;
even so, you have indeed forgotten your own true nature through limiting adjuncts. You are that very Reality, the Supreme Brahman—remember your state of perfection.

From the specific signs of withering in a tree deprived of life, one knows that there exists a supreme Self, subtle and eternal, and that it is one; know this entire world to have that as its essence, devoid of any second unreal thing—“Thou art That,” the true reality of Being; abandon the delusion of duality. 52.
Within the grain, there once again appeared that most exalted banyan tree, within which this entire world was situated;
that subtle Brahman, subtler than the subtle, which is to be realized by the faithful—you are That, the Truth; all else is unreal. 53.
That which is not seen by the eye nor even by the senses, yet shines within the heart;
that which is realized through the Guru’s instruction as if one perceives flavor with the tongue—that is the True Brahman, and you are That. But this visible world is not you. 54.
Like a man abandoned in the forest by thieves, you have had your pure vision bound within bodies by passion and other afflictions;
yet like a traveler whose bonds have been released by a master, you are the venerable Brahman—attain your own abode in happiness. 55.
Wherein the deluded one, having attained [death] through the process of dissolution of the organs and so forth, dies and returns again to the succession of births;
but the wise man, with delusion cast aside, evades death—[realizing] "Thou art That," the true Brahman—cross over the bondage of death! 56.
A person of deluded intellect, intent on falsehood, experiences burning and bondage like a thief before a heated axe;
but when one whose intent is truth is no longer distressed by the thought "Thou art That"—the Self which is the Reality of the Existent Brahman—then cast away the fear of bondage. 57.
Thus enlightened by his father with these well-spoken words, the son realized his own Self as the solid mass of non-dual bliss and the awakening of Truth.
Reflecting upon this, even one who has known the supreme vision of non-duality shall attain the happiness of self-sovereignty and become one who has fulfilled his purpose. 58.
Having conceived the oneness of the entire universe within the Praṇava, and having divided it into parts and dissolved them, what remains is that single Self;
"This world is the Self, it is a delusion"—thus the speech of the Atharva Veda makes it perfectly clear. 59.

I am the inner Brahman—eternal, pure, awakened, devoid of transformation, eternally free by nature, truth, subtle, free from duality, partless, full, and of the nature of bliss. Just as darkness does not exist, nor remains, nor will ever exist in the sun which is its own natural light, so too this entire universe does not exist, nor remains, nor will ever exist in me, who am the self-luminous light of bliss and unattached. 60.

Thus, from the friction of the fire-drill that is the reflected statement, she is immediately born like a spark of fire; having burnt away the entire web of duality along with delusion as if it were a blade of grass, she—being eternally established in the reality of the Self which is unsurpassed bliss known as liberation—suddenly goes to destruction, just as the mud of a river vanishes when the water rises.

This is indeed the perfect medical treatment for the disease of worldly existence—an irregular fever of the three beginningless torments; it is the milch-cow that yields the mass of supreme bliss consisting of self-sovereignty.

Furthermore, once the seed of karma has been reduced to ashes by this [treatment], it is no longer able to sprout; and the severing of the knot of doubt is also declared to occur through the attainment of this. 62.
The section on refutation is complete.
Now begins the section on absolute liberation (*kaivalya*):
"The indivisible cognition, having as its object the reality that is directly perceived, does not abandon its directness even when produced by words."
Having carefully heard such words as "You are the tenth," he certainly does not wish to perceive himself [as such]. || 1 ||
Nor does an object that is directly perceived even by itself become indirect merely because it is known through a cognition produced by words.
Indeed, there is no difference in the nature of the object as it appears between what is illuminated by a lamp and what is illuminated by the sun. (2)
A cognition regarding an object that is not directly perceived cannot be considered a lack of valid means of knowledge;
for since the Self is eternally manifest by its very nature, even a skillful person is unable to conceal it, however much they might wish to do so. (3)

Because there is no perception of objects of pleasure, pain, or passion when one is indifferent, or when one is blinded by darkness or asleep—therefore, the fitness of this object, which is its capacity for being perceived, constitutes its immediacy; it is not determined by the sense organs.
Moreover, for one whose object is a concealed reality, the darkness [of ignorance] is experienced as being shattered by the word, which produces indirect knowledge (parokṣadhī);
yet, after describing that [reality] through mere instruction, the Śruti further says, "He shows the further shore. (5)
And you ordain that hearing which, having investigated the scope of the Upanishads, leads to the vision of the Supreme Self;
for even Janaka, whose darkness had been dispelled by mere hearing, said of you: "You ferry me across to the further shore. 6.

The immediacy of consciousness is primary for that which is self-luminous and perceived by itself, being independent of anything else; it is secondary regarding objects within its range that are free from obscuration and identical with it.
As for external objects, a mental modification (vṛtti) produced by the senses is required to effect a connection with consciousness.
The manifestation of consciousness arising from the sentence dispels mere delusion, independent of anything else. || 7 ||

In order to shatter the non-awakening of consciousness regarding an object, or rather to produce an attachment to an object, the mind is intended to be brought to the form of that object; thus, the path of the contact between the object and the senses proceeds outside the body. (8)

That which is not to be seen by the eyes and other senses, by which these objects are kindled as their respective referents; that which is not the domain of speech and the rest, by which the group of speech and so forth is repeatedly set in motion;

by which the vital breath is led forth, and by which the body, organs, mind, and intellect are ignited—that pure Self is established by itself, free from duality, fearless, consisting of consciousness, being, and bliss. 9.

Even for one who has been thus instructed, if awakening does not occur because the mind is inattentive, he should—through the power of a passion for further reflection, with the aid of the virtuous, and by his own effort—restrain the senses and even the fickle mind, either through gentle coaxing or by force, to pacify its distractions; then, in solitude, he should meditate upon the one Infinite Self, whose nature is supreme bliss and consciousness. 10.

Having abandoned attachment, being patient, pure, eating what is wholesome and in moderation, perceiving the meaning of the Yoga scriptures, firm in the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), established in his own posture, and serene;

having withdrawn the restless mind through the process of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and restraining it from both the gross and the subtle, he meditates. With his mind stabilized in the bliss of non-duality, he severs the bond of delusion. 11.

Whether one has ascended to the experience of the Supreme Self—the boundless consciousness and ground of infinite bliss—through the words of scripture, or whether one possesses firm meditative absorption, or even if one engages with the multitude of sense objects while gathering the world together, let there be no further bondage. 12.
Even if as many four-faced Brahmās as there are atoms in the earth were to pass away without attaining it,
there would be no gain superior to the attainment of one’s own Self— that ocean of uninterrupted bliss free from suffering.
If it were non-existent, it would be sublated due to its dissimilarity with that which has been destroyed; furthermore, the sublation of delusion is not some other form of destruction.
Moreover, the cognition of sublation would not be a mere manifestation of absence, or else even absence must have the nature of the underlying substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). || 14 ||
The entire mass of accumulated karma quickly turns to ashes by the fire of awakening;
this radiant awakening is not touched by karma, just as a flame is not obscured by the smoke of its own fuel. || 15 ||

Just as cloth remains in the form of cloth even when it is being burned, due to the fear produced by that burning, and just as ashes remain in the form of cloth even when the cloth has been destroyed, so too for the wise, the universe persists until the fall of the body, capable of providing the experience of prārabdha karma, even though it is sublated by their own [realization]. || 17 ||
Even while living, he has no notion of a self in this body, just as a snake has none in a withered vine;
if, through mere delusion, he were to imagine a state of being an embodied soul in the Supreme, what loss would that be for him here? (18)
Even all the gods and asuras, though striving with every effort, cannot prevail against one who has realized the truth for his own ruin;
for who indeed could act against his own welfare? Yet this ascetic is the very self of even them. (19)
Due to the destruction of defects such as passion, greed, and negligence, he never engages in misconduct anywhere;
intent on protecting virtuous conduct like a mother protects her child, he proceeds by the path of the righteous through his refined character.

Having attained further pleasure, he does not exult; as immovable as Mount Meru even amidst great hardships, he gladdens his own self by means of the Self and wanders the earth like a god, filled with bliss.
Some are devoted to the conduct of their caste and stage of life, while others are like deluded children or intoxicated men;
some are full of passion, some are seekers of enjoyment, and others are practitioners of yoga—the state of those who possess knowledge is observed to be manifold in form. || 22 ||

May the various, secret, and wonderful movements of yogis—who always sport in their own innate bliss, indulging in spontaneous play, free from attachment and unimpeded, bringing about a mass of welfare for the worlds—be difficult to perceive, like that of fish in water, birds in the sky, or the wind at the face of the quarters. 23.
"May I be purified by the dust of the feet of Hari, the Lord of the three worlds, whose lotus feet are meditated upon by yogis, and who is himself eternally peaceful"—thus he spoke.
Who else here is more blessed than he, whose mind is unwaveringly immersed in self-bliss, and whose lotus feet are bowed to by gods, asuras, and men, that teacher of the universe? (24)
Though his desires were thus fulfilled, he wandered the earth out of innate curiosity, devoted to the welfare of all and tasting his own bliss at every step;
having reached the further shore of the ocean of the snare of delusion with wonder, curiosity, compassion, joy, and longing, the steadfast one sings thus repeatedly: 25.
Ah! After being submerged for a long time in the ocean of birth, so treacherous by nature, I have finally obtained through my merits a Guru who is a wish-fulfilling jewel of nectar;
by whose pure and sweet rays I now delight in that stainless, self-perfected abode of infinite bliss.
Just as before, when my vision was clouded by illusion, I did not perceive the innate state even while seeing my own self-manifested happiness;
so now, with eyes purified by the collyrium of knowledge, though I see this world within the space of consciousness, I do not perceive it as a false reality. 27.
Neither knowable nor unknowable, delightful by its own innate essence, a mass of bliss, neither expressible in prose nor to be set aside, nor to be surpassed in any way;
neither to be rejected nor to be accepted, nor even to be concealed for a moment—oh, this Self, suddenly bursting forth, obscures this entire world of ours! 28.
What has set? What has been destroyed? What has been tossed about? Or what has dissolved? Has it fallen apart, or has it been swallowed, or indeed instantly digested?
When my own mind is calm within me—in that vast, unimpeded, and independent ocean of incomparable, innate bliss—I do not perceive this entire world at all.
How did this come to be? How indeed does it persist, and how does it go to dissolution?
Having thoroughly investigated the universe within my own stainless vision, free from attachment, I am at peace, realizing that it is all false.

How does that supreme, uncreated [Brahman]—which is supportless in form, devoid of constituent parts and configuration, immovable, effortless, free from dualities, and the glory of its own incomparable bliss—fashion the collection of the three worlds without employing any means or its own assembly of instruments? || 31 ||
He has no prosperity, nor ministers, nor indeed objects of the senses, nor horses; his treasuries are not full, nor are there settlements of cities, nor friends.
And yet, alone with himself, having conquered the wretched army of his enemies by his own strength, he protects this entire world—this is truly a marvel.

Unattached and indifferent, nourished by the supreme bliss of its own essence, free from hunger, with consciousness as its body and lacking hands, feet, or a belly—though devoid of illusion and being the Self itself, and though inherently without space, how and why, alas, does it suddenly swallow the three worlds along with their illusions? 33.
Repeatedly deluded, I have utterly squandered my vast accumulation of wealth; I have no one to trust, nor do I fear even the rod of Yama.
Hating virtue and loving only my own self-interest, my conduct is intent on deceiving the world, yet no one anywhere perceives this strange reality.
Neither my father, nor my mother, nor even my friend is my abode; neither food nor drink, nor the ever-moving wind, nor even the sky is my home.
Alas, though I wander through the entire world, no one perceives me! Oh, what a wretched state it is for me that even this incomparable sovereignty of happiness eludes me! 35.
The world is not real for me, nor indeed is it my home; the lotus is untouched by dust, and the word "treasure" has no power over me.
There is no association with new speech, nor any addiction to the creation of discordant compositions; nevertheless, I am Brahmā, and I utter that collection of Vedas.
I am neither a magician, nor one who reclines upon the serpent-king, nor a wielder of the discus, nor one who has taken the ten incarnations;
I have no web of illusion to be maintained, yet I am Viṣṇu, the all-powerful Lord.
I have no eightfold forms, nor am I uneven; I have no [third] eye, no smearing with ashes, and no movement upon a bull.
I have no association with serpents, nor any frustration of my desires; nevertheless, I am manifest as the Supreme Śiva himself. 39.
Though plunging into the forest of waking, sleeping, and dreaming, he remains unattached; due to the excellence of his being, he cannot be perceived by the outward-looking deer of the senses.
Having quelled the herd of intoxicated elephants of great delusion through the playful movement of his conduct, may that lion of our own Self sport in the state that transcends time. 40.

Thus, with these rays that dispel the world's dullness—rays that are truly radiant, pleasing to the ear, and awakening like nectar—he gladdens those who bow at every step; being awakened, he purifies the directions, just as the sun does. 41.

Blessed indeed is he who has most fully accomplished his purpose; blessed indeed is his lineage, for he, having cast off the shackles of karma, has fixed his mind on the fearless Self—the essence of the Vedas—and dwells in peace.
Having dwelt in this manner for a very long time, his desires fully realized, he— expert in rescuing those fallen into the flood of compassion,
with all sorrow departed upon the exhaustion of the remnants of his past karma— remains as an ocean of the bliss of self-sovereignty, free from all limiting conditions.

Neither rising nor setting, neither increasing nor undergoing diminution, kindled by its own radiance, ever full with the innate nectar of bliss, and free from all blemish—this indescribable moon of one’s own Self shines forth. 44.

May that Supreme Person, who consists of pure consciousness, be eternally victorious— he who is an ocean of the nectar of universal bliss, a fire of sparks of all-encompassing knowledge, a concealed sword-blade within the sheath that cuts through the delusion of duality, a sun for the darkness of ignorance, and a crest-jewel upon the head of the lady of Vedānta.

May this *Svārājyasiddhi* bring joy to the wise—those adorned with the divine jewels of peace and other virtues, who long for the nectar of the ocean of Vedānta, and who have taken refuge at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree of liberation (*kaivalya*). 46.
May this handful of flowers of speech, offered with devotion at the feet of Śiva and Śivā, who inspire the intellect, lead to the attainment of their pleasure. 47.
The section on Isolation is complete.
